pages.text: Mr Anim gave Kwadwo a single thin stick. “Break it,” he said. Snap! It broke easily. Then he handed Kwadwo a tight bundle of sticks tied together. “Now break this.” Kwadwo pushed and pulled, but the bundle would not break. “That,” said Mr Anim, “is the story of the Asante union.”

pages.text: “By the 1680s, several large Akan kingdoms had grown up in the forest,” said Mr Anim. “In the last years of the seventeenth century, a powerful state called Denkyira conquered them and ruled them harshly. The smaller states were strong alone, but not strong enough to resist.”

“In the last years of the seventeenth century, a powerful state called Denkyira conquered them and ruled them harshly.
The smaller states were strong alone, but not strong enough to resist.”
pages.alt: A map of the forest region with a large kingdom in the middle and smaller ones around it.

pages.text: “Around Kwaaman, which became Kumasi, a group of Oyoko clans had settled,” said Mr Anim. “A leader named Osei Tutu and his priest and adviser, Okomfo Anokye, led them in bringing the states together. They agreed to stand as one, under a shared law and a shared symbol, to throw off Denkyira rule.”

pages.alt: Chiefs and elders stand in a circle in front of a shared stool.

pages.text: “There is a saying that the name Asante means because of war,” said Mr Anim. Esther raised her hand. “Is that certain?” “It is one explanation people give,” he said. “Names often have more than one story. I will tell you what I know and tell you when I am not sure.”

I will tell you what I know and tell you when I am not sure.”

pages.text: “The decisive fight took place at Feyiase,” said Mr Anim. “The Denkyira king, Ntim Gyakari, was killed, and the Asante captured the cannons Denkyira had brought. The Asante had few firearms of their own, but they won. Denkyira rule was broken. And here is a puzzle: one source gives the date as August 1701, and another says 1700. I will not choose for you.”

pages.text: “The Golden Stool, Sika Dwa Kofi, became the seal of the union,” said Mr Anim. “Asante tradition says Okomfo Anokye called it down from the sky. We learned last term that this belongs to tradition, and that we handle it with respect. What matters here is that it stood for all the member states together, not for one town.”

What matters here is that it stood for all the member states together, not for one town.”
pages.alt: A golden stool, drawn respectfully on its own cloth, with chiefs standing around it.

pages.text: “The union also had rules,” said Mr Anim. “It had a council and an army arranged in wings, each state with its own duties. There was an annual festival called Odwira. A strict law forbade people to bring up the old conquests and origins of member states, because the leaders wanted unity to be more important than old quarrels.”

pages.text: “Between 1700 and 1750,” said Mr Anim, “the union grew until it covered an area bigger than modern Ghana.” Kwadwo held up the bundle. “One stick breaks, but many together do not.” “That is the lesson, and the history,” said Mr Anim. Esther added, “And also: always check the date.” Everyone laughed. The end.

activities.question: Why did the states join together?
options: To free themselves from Denkyira rule

activities.prompt: Mr Anim says he will tell the class when he is not sure. Why is that a good habit for a historian?

activities.definition: A group of people or states joined together for a shared purpose.

items: Denkyira conquered the smaller Akan states.
The states agreed to stand together in a union.
The union defeated Denkyira at Feyiase.
The union grew to cover a large area.

activities.prompt: Many people working together can do what one cannot. When did you last succeed by working with others?

glossary.definition: A group of states or people joined together for a shared purpose.
